answer.worked:
Let $u=\sin x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{du}{dx}&=\cos x\\dx&=\frac{du}{\cos x}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$, $u=0$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, $u=\frac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\pi/6}\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\,dx&=\int_0^{1/2}\frac{1}{1+u}\,du\\&=\left[\ln|1+u|\right]_0^{1/2}\\&=\ln\left(\frac32\right)-\ln1\\&=\ln\left(\frac32\right)\end{aligned}$$

Let $u=\sin x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{du}{dx}&=\cos x\\dx&=\frac{du}{\cos x}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$, $u=0$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $u=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin^2x}\,dx&=\int_0^1\frac{1}{1+u^2}\,du\\&=\left[\tan^{-1}u\right]_0^1\\&=\frac\pi4-0\\&=\frac\pi4\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{du}{dx}&=\cos x\\dx&=\frac{du}{\cos x}\\\cos^2x&=1-u^2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$, $u=0$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $u=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^3x\,dx&=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2x\cos x\,dx\\&=\int_0^1(1-u^2)\,du\\&=\left[u-\frac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\&=1-\frac13\\&=\frac23\end{aligned}$$

Let $u=\sin x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{du}{dx}&=\cos x\\dx&=\frac{du}{\cos x}\\\cos^2x&=1-u^2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, $u=\frac{1}{2}$; when $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $u=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^3x}{\sin^4x}\,dx&=\int_{1/2}^1\frac{1-u^2}{u^4}\,du\\&=\int_{1/2}^1(u^{-4}-u^{-2})\,du\\&=\left[-\frac{1}{3u^3}+\frac1u\right]_{1/2}^1\\&=\left(-\frac13+1\right)-\left(-\frac83+2\right)\\&=\frac43\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx$ using three different methods and confirm you get the same answer.

answer.worked:
Let $u=1+x^2$, so $du=2x\,dx$ and $dx=\dfrac{du}{2x}$.

Limits: when $x=0$, $u=1$; when $x=1$, $u=2$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx&=\frac12\int_1^2u^{-1/2}\,du\\&=\frac12\left[2\sqrt u\right]_1^2\\&=\left[\sqrt u\right]_1^2\\&=\sqrt2-1.\end{aligned}$$

Let $x^2=t$, so $x=\sqrt t$ and $dx=\dfrac{dt}{2\sqrt t}$.

Limits: when $x=0$, $t=0$; when $x=1$, $t=1$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx&=\int_0^1\left(\frac{\sqrt t}{\sqrt{1+t}}\cdot\frac1{2\sqrt t}\right)\,dt\\&=\frac12\int_0^1(1+t)^{-1/2}\,dt\\&=\frac12\left[2\sqrt{1+t}\right]_0^1\\&=\left[\sqrt{1+t}\right]_0^1\\&=\sqrt2-1.\end{aligned}$$

Let $x=\tan\theta$, so $dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{1+x^2}=\sec\theta$ on $0\leq\theta\leq\dfrac\pi4$.

Limits: when $x=0$, $\theta=0$; when $x=1$, $\theta=\dfrac\pi4$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta}\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\\&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta\\&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin\theta(\cos\theta)^{-2}\,d\theta\\&=\left[(\cos\theta)^{-1}\right]_0^{\pi/4}\\&=\frac1{\cos(\pi/4)}-\frac1{\cos0}\\&=\sqrt2-1.\end{aligned}$$

All three methods give $\sqrt2-1$.

content.prompt: Find the equation of $y=f(x)$ if $f'(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x$ and $f(3)=0$. Use $x=3\sec\theta$.

answer.worked:
We are trying to find $f(x)=\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,dx=\int\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x\,dx$.

Let $x=3\sec\theta$, with $0\leq\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. Then $dx=3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x^2-9}&=\sqrt{9\sec^2\theta-9}\\&=\sqrt{9\tan^2\theta}\\&=3\tan\theta.\end{aligned}$$

Also simplify
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x\\&=\frac{3\tan\theta}{3\sec\theta}\\&=\sin\theta.\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x\,dx\\&=\int\sin\theta\cdot3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\\&=3\int\tan^2\theta\,d\theta\\&=3\int(\sec^2\theta-1)\,d\theta\\&=3(\tan\theta-\theta)+C.\end{aligned}$$

Here $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}3$ and $\theta=\sec^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac x3\right)$, where $\sec^{-1}$ denotes inverse secant. Hence
$$f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-9}-3\sec^{-1}\!\left(\frac x3\right)+C.$$

Substitute $f(3)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=0-3(0)+C\\C&=0.\end{aligned}$$

Therefore $f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-9}-3\sec^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac x3\right)$ on the branch $x\geq3$.

answer.worked:
Let $u = \cos^2 x$. 
Differentiating with respect to $x$:
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{du}{dx} &= -2\cos x \sin x \\
&= -\sin 2x
\end{align*}$$
So, $du = -\sin 2x \, dx$, which means $\sin 2x \, dx = -du$.
Now, find the new limits of integration:
When $x = 0$:
$$\begin{align*}
u &= \cos^2(0) = 1^2 = 1
\end{align*}$$
When $x = \frac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{align*}
u &= \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}
\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the integral:
$$\begin{align*}
\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sin 2x}{4+\cos^2 x} \, dx &= \int_1^{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{-du}{4+u} \\
&= \int_{\frac{1}{2}}^1 \frac{1}{4+u} \, du \\
&= \left[ \ln(4+u) \right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^1 \\
&= \ln(4+1) - \ln\left(4+\frac{1}{2}\right) \\
&= \ln 5 - \ln\left(\frac{9}{2}\right) \\
&= \ln\left(\frac{5}{\frac{9}{2}}\right) \\

\end{align*}$$

Using the substitution $u^2=x+1$ where $u>0$ to find:
$$\int_0^3 \frac{x+2}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx$$

answer.worked:
Since $u^2=x+1$ and $u>0$:
$$\begin{align*}

dx &= 2u\,du

Changing the limits:
$$\begin{align*}

&= \left[\frac{2u^3}{3}+2u\right]_1^2 \\
&= \left(\frac{16}{3}+4\right)-\left(\frac{2}{3}+2\right) \\
&= \frac{20}{3}
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Let $f(x)$ be a continuous function with $a > 0$ and $k > 0$.
Which of the following is true?
(A) $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x) \, dx = k \int_0^{ak} f(kx) \, dx$
(B) $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x) \, dx = \frac{1}{k} \int_0^{ak} f(kx) \, dx$
(C) $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x) \, dx = k \int_0^{ak} f\left(\frac{x}{k}\right) \, dx$
(D) $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x) \, dx = \frac{1}{k} \int_0^{ak} f\left(\frac{x}{k}\right) \, dx$

answer.worked:
Consider $\dfrac1k\displaystyle\int_0^{ak} f\left(\frac xk\right)dx$ with $u=\dfrac xk$.

Then $du=\dfrac1k\,dx$. When $x=0,\ u=0$; when $x=ak,\ u=a$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac1k\int_0^{ak} f\left(\frac xk\right)dx&=\int_0^a f(u)\,du\\&=\int_0^a f(x)\,dx\end{align*}$$
This matches the left-hand side, so the answer is (D).

answer.worked:
$x=3\sin\theta$, so $dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta$.

When $x=0,\ \theta=0$; when $x=\frac{3}{\sqrt2},\ \theta=\frac\pi4$. On this interval $\cos\theta>0$.
$$\begin{align*}\int_0^{3/\sqrt2}\frac{dx}{(9-x^2)^{3/2}}&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{3\cos\theta}{(9\cos^2\theta)^{3/2}}\,d\theta\\&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{3\cos\theta}{27\cos^3\theta}\,d\theta\\&=\frac19\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\\&=\frac19\left[\tan\theta\right]_0^{\pi/4}\\&=\frac19\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Using the substitution $u=-x$, or otherwise, evaluate
$$\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2x}{1+2^x}\,dx.$$

answer.worked:
Let $I=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2x}{1+2^x}\,dx$.

Under $u=-x$, $du=-dx$ and the limits swap, so
$$\begin{align*}I&=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2u}{1+2^{-u}}\,du\\&=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{2^u\sin^2u}{1+2^u}\,du.\end{align*}$$
Adding the two forms,
$$\begin{align*}2I&=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^2x\,dx\\&=\frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(1-\cos 2x)\,dx\\&=\frac12\left[x-\frac12\sin 2x\right]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\\&=\frac\pi2.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $I=\dfrac\pi4$.

content.prompt:
Given that $a=3^{-1/6}$ and $b=3^{1/6}$, using the substitution $u=\frac1x$ or otherwise, evaluate
$$\int_a^b\frac{x^3}{(1+x)(1+x^6)}\,dx.$$

answer.worked:
Let
$$I=\int_a^b\frac{x^3}{(1+x)(1+x^6)}\,dx.$$
With $u=1/x$, the limits interchange and simplification gives
$$I=\int_a^b\frac{x^2}{(1+x)(1+x^6)}\,dx.$$
Adding the two forms,
$$\begin{align*}
2I &= \int_a^b\frac{x^3+x^2}{(1+x)(1+x^6)}\,dx \\
&= \int_a^b\frac{x^2}{1+x^6}\,dx \\
&= \frac13\left[\tan^{-1}(x^3)\right]_a^b \\
&= \frac13\left(\tan^{-1}\sqrt3-\tan^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt3}\right) \\
&= \frac{\pi}{18}.
\end{align*}$$
Therefore $I=\dfrac{\pi}{36}$.

entries.description:
When a function is reflected across the line y = x to produce its inverse, two things happen:
1. Each point (a,b) on the original curve maps to (b,a) on the inverse.

entries.description:
y = sin⁻¹ x for −π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2
sin y = x for −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2
dx/dy = cos y
dy/dx = 1/(cos y)

We want to change cos y to an expression in terms of x. Since x = sin y, we first write cos y in terms of sin y.

sin² y + cos² y = 1
cos y = ±√(1 − sin² y)
        = ±√(1 − x²)

since −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2, cos y ≥ 0

∴ cos y = √(1 − x²)
∴ dy/dx = 1/√(1 − x²)

entries.description: We are trying to find \(f(x)=\int f'(x)\,dx=\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x\,dx\). Let \(x=3\sec\theta\). \(dx=3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\); \(\sqrt{x^2-9}=\sqrt{9\sec^2\theta-9}=\sqrt{9(\tan^2\theta)}=3\tan\theta\). Therefore \(f(x)=\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}x\,dx=\int\sin\theta\cdot3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta=3\int\tan^2\theta\,d\theta=3\int(\sec^2\theta-1)\,d\theta=3(\tan\theta-\theta)+C\). \(\tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}3\), \(\theta=\sec^{-1}(x/3)\). Hence \(f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-9}-3\sec^{-1}(x/3)+C\). Substitute \(f(3)=0\): \(0=0-3(0)+C\), therefore \(C=0\). Therefore \(f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-9}-3\sec^{-1}(x/3)\).
